evidence: 1000-Word Philosophy: philosophers consider broader, more fundamental questions; physicists ask what caused some event, philosophers ask whether causation even exists; whether a law is fair or just.

1000-Word Philosophy: philosophical questions can't be investigated through purely empirical means (a lab experiment on equality over freedom); philosophers often incorporate scientific knowledge as premises.
IEP Argument: the reasons offered are premises and the proposition they support is the conclusion; 1000-Word Philosophy: the main method of academic philosophy is to construct and evaluate arguments.
1000-Word Philosophy: when a topic becomes amenable to rigorous empirical study it tends to be outsourced to its own field; the natural sciences were once called natural philosophy.
1000-Word Philosophy: most of the different doctoral degrees are called Doctor of Philosophy even when they're in sociology or chemistry.
SEP Buddha: fl. circa 450 BCE; SEP Confucius: trad. 551-479 BCE; IEP Thales: c. 620 to c. 546 BCE.
1000-Word Philosophy: metaphysicians study what sorts of entities exist, what the world and its constituents are made of, and how objects or events might cause or explain each other.
SEP Epistemology: the term comes from episteme (knowledge) and logos; 1000-Word Philosophy: epistemologists study knowledge, evidence and justified belief, e.g. whether we can trust our senses.
1000-Word Philosophy, value theory: What makes wrong actions wrong? How do we identify good people and good lives?
1000-Word Philosophy: logicians study good and bad arguments and reasoning.
IEP Aesthetics: may be defined narrowly as the theory of beauty, or more broadly as that together with the philosophy of art.
IEP Political Philosophy: begins with the question what ought to be a person's relationship to society; 1000-Word Philosophy: what makes a society just or unjust?

SEP Metaphysics: Aristotle did not know the word; at least one hundred years after his death an editor (in all probability Andronicus of Rhodes) titled the books Ta meta ta phusika, the ones after the physical ones.
SEP Thought Experiments: basically devices of the imagination; used in many disciplines including biology, economics, history, mathematics, philosophy and physics.
SEP: the Aristotelian account holds heavy bodies fall faster; a heavy cannon ball and light musket ball attached together should fall both slower and faster, a contradiction.
Republic (Jowett, Gutenberg): the shepherd finds the ring, becomes invisible, is sent to court, seduced the queen, and with her help conspired against the king and slew him, and took the kingdom.

Republic (Jowett): suppose two such magic rings, the just put on one and the unjust the other; the actions of the just would be as the actions of the unjust; no one is just willingly but from necessity.

Internet Archive record for Real People (1988): Wilkes argues thought-experimentation engenders inconclusive and unconvincing results, then examines real-life conditions; SEP names her skeptical challenge to personal identity scenarios.
IEP Plato: the world we know through the senses is only an imitation of the pure, eternal and unchanging world of the Forms.

SEP Plato: the most fundamental distinction in Plato's philosophy is between the many observable objects that appear beautiful and the one object that is what beauty really is; IEP: participation or sharing.
SEP Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics: the Circle Itself is perfectly circular; a drawn circle, or a round ball, is deficient in that it is not perfectly circular.
IEP Plato: the Forms or Ideas exist in a supra-sensible realm available only to thought.
SEP Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics: in the Phaedo Plato shows we cannot have acquired knowledge of the Form Equality from perceptual encounters, using the example of equal sticks.

SEP Plato's Parmenides 4.3: Plato never refers to any argument as the Third Man; the moniker derives from Aristotle; IEP Plato: considerable controversy over whether Plato believed the theory vulnerable to it.

SEP Aristotle on Causality: we think we have knowledge of a thing only when we have grasped its cause; the search for causes was a search for answers to why; all four causes may enter the explanation of something.
SEP: the bronze enters in the explanation of the production of the statue as the material cause.
SEP: the bronze is melted and poured to acquire a new shape, the shape of the statue; this shape enters the explanation as the formal cause.
SEP: the efficient cause is the principle that produces the statue; for Aristotle this principle is the art of bronze-casting (Phys. II 3), which resides in the artisan.
SEP: a model is made, a mold prepared, the bronze melted and poured, all for the sake of a certain end, the production of the statue.

SEP Aristotle's Metaphysics: the bronze and the roundness are not two separate things; IEP Aristotle: joined the Academy studying under Plato for twenty years; On Ideas collected arguments against Platonic forms.

Advancement of Learning (Gutenberg): metaphysic handles formal and final causes; 'the clouds are for watering of the earth' is well inquired in metaphysic, but in physic impertinent, remoras that have caused the search of physical causes to be neglected.
SEP Confucius: trad. 551-479 BCE; the Analects depicts Confucius teaching and conversing with disciples and is the traditional main source.
SEP Chinese Ethics: the word junzi originally meant prince's son, but in the Analects it refers to ethical nobility.
SEP Chinese Ethics: the first English translations rendered junzi as gentleman, but Ames and Rosemont (1998) have usefully suggested exemplary person.
SEP Chinese Ethics: in the narrower sense ren is explained in 12.22 in terms of caring for others; translations include benevolence.

SEP Chinese Ethics: before Confucius ren referred to the aristocracy of bloodlines, something like the strong and handsome appearance of an aristocrat; in the Analects a moral excellence anyone can achieve.

SEP Confucius: li, ritual propriety, connotes the conventions of ritual and etiquette, down to rules such as avoiding garments with red-black trim (10.6); SEP Chinese Ethics quotes 12.1 on restraining yourself and returning to the rites.

Analects (Legge) 3.26: ceremonies performed without reverence; mourning conducted without sorrow; wherewith should I contemplate such ways? 3.4: in mourning, better deep sorrow than minute attention to observances.
SEP Mohism: the ren person avoids extravagant funerals and prolonged mourning (customs promoted by the Ru); wealth, a large population and social order are the goods the benevolent person desires.
SEP Laozi: flourished during the sixth century BCE according to Chinese sources; according to some modern scholars Laozi is entirely legendary; the name means Old Master.
SEP Laozi: the etymology of the Chinese graph suggests a pathway; most commentators translate dao as way.
Legge, Tao Teh King ch. 1: 'The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.'
SEP Laozi: some translators opt for effortless action; wuwei does not mean total inaction; in the Laozi it is a contrast against any form of action driven by self-serving desire.

Legge ch. 8: the highest excellence is like water, benefiting all things and occupying without striving the low place which all men dislike; ch. 78: nothing more soft and weak than water, yet for attacking the firm and strong nothing takes precedence of it.

Zhuangzi (Giles tr.): a good cook changes his chopper once a year, an ordinary cook once a month; I have had this chopper nineteen years and its edge is as if fresh, since at the joints there are always interstices.
IEP Zhuangzi: Chuang-Tzu, 369-298 BCE.
Legge ch. 38: when righteousness was lost, the proprieties appeared; propriety is the attenuated form of leal-heartedness and good faith, and is also the commencement of disorder.
IEP Zhuangzi: Xunzi mentions Zhuangzi by name as recognizing the value of nature but thereby failing to recognize the value of the human.
SEP Buddha: the Buddha does deny that any of the psychophysical elements is a self; all of classical Indian philosophy, Buddhist and orthodox alike, understood him to have denied the self tout court.
SEP Mind in Indian Buddhist Philosophy: five aggregates: material form or body, sensations, apperception, volitions or dispositional formations, and consciousness.
SEP Buddha: mental events and psychophysical elements are impermanent, so they fail to account for a persisting self; the Buddha denies any of them is a self.
SEP: the dialogue between the Buddhist philosopher Nagasena and King Milinda (often identified with the Greco-Bactrian King Menander I, ca. 150 BCE).

Rhys Davids tr.: Nagasena is only a generally understood term, a designation in common use, for there is no permanent individuality; the king: Nagasena is a mere empty sound... it is a falsehood that your reverence has spoken.

Rhys Davids tr.: Is it the pole... the axle... the wheels...? all these parts? anything outside them? No each time; the king: on account of its having all these things it comes under the designation in common use of chariot.
SEP Buddha: the stock example of a conventionally real entity is the chariot, real only because it is more convenient to have a single name for the parts when assembled in the right way.

IEP Nyaya: Uddyotakara, following Vatsyayana, argues that if I am now a different self than the me of yesterday, I should not be able to recollect what that me experienced; Indian Philosophy Blog: Buddhists explain memory by transmission from one momentary dharma to the next.
IEP Nyaya: the oldest extant Nyaya text is the Nyaya-sutra attributed to Gautama (c. 200 CE).
IEP Nyaya: the four pramanas are perception, inference, analogy (comparison) and testimony.
IEP Nyaya stock example: there is fire on the hill, because there is smoke on the hill; wherever there is smoke there is fire, like a kitchen hearth and unlike a lake.

IEP Advaita Vedanta: Shankara is regarded as the promoter of Advaita; as many scholars believe he lived in the eighth century; the experiencing self and atman are in reality identical (both are Brahman).
IEP Indian Materialism: the Lokayata (Carvaka) school recognized perception alone as a reliable source of knowledge, rejecting inference and testimony as commonly held pramanas.
IEP Indian Materialism: even human consciousness is a material construct; body is the substratum of consciousness.
IEP Jain Philosophy: reality is multifaceted (anekanta) such that no one view can capture it in its entirety, illustrated by the famous story of the blind men trying to describe an elephant.
Legge ch. 3: when there is this abstinence from action, good order is universal; SEP Confucius: Confucius associated with training scholar-officials and texts important to rulers.
IEP Nyaya defends the diachronic existence of selves against Buddhist views; IEP Advaita: jiva and atman are in reality identical (Brahman); SEP Buddha: the Buddha denied the self.
SEP Ibn Sina: Ibn-Sina [Avicenna] (ca. 970-1037) was the preeminent philosopher and physician of the Islamic world.

Adamson and Benevich tr. of On the Soul: created all at once, and created as perfect, sight prevented from seeing, hovering in the air or a void so it does not feel it, limbs separated so they do not meet.
Adamson and Benevich tr.: he has no doubt that his essence is existent, while not affirming any limb, nor his heart or his brain, nor any length, width or depth.
SEP Self-Consciousness: Avicenna's Flying Man with all senses disabled would be self-aware; thus the self one cognises cannot be a bodily thing of which one is aware through the senses.
Adamson and Benevich, citing Kaukua: the thought experiment moves from an opaque to a transparent context; one can affirm Cicero without affirming Tully, so the soul might in fact be the body.
SEP al-Ghazali (c. 1056-1111), prominent thinker of Sunni Islam; critique of twenty positions of falsafa in the Incoherence; the falasifa claimed demonstrative proof (burhan).
SEP al-Ghazali: the longest and most substantial discussion is the first, on Avicenna's and al-Farabi's arguments for the world's pre-eternity; al-Ghazali denies this can be demonstrated.
SEP al-Ghazali: observation points towards a concomitant occurrence but not to an occurrence through it; the connection between cause and effect is not necessary.

IEP quotes the Incoherence: the one who enacts the burning is God; as for fire, which is inanimate, it has no action; SEP: by creating combustion every time fire touches cotton, God follows a custom (ada).
IEP Ibn Rushd (1126-1198): born in Cordova, jurist and physician; Tahafut al-Tahafut (Incoherence of the Incoherence) answers al-Ghazali; SEP gives the same dates.
SEP quotes ITI 318-19: something may hinder the action of fire, as is asserted of talc, but one need not therefore deny fire its burning power.

Van den Bergh tr.: the philosophers believe there are four causes: agent, matter, form and end; intelligence is nothing but the perception of things with their causes; denial of cause implies the denial of knowledge.
SEP Maimonides (1138-1204): born in Cordova, Spain in 1138; arrived in Egypt in 1166 and settled in Fustat, a section of Cairo.
SEP: the Guide of the Perplexed was completed in 1190; ostensibly a letter written to an advanced student who cannot decide whether to follow philosophy or the teachings of his religion.
SEP: the Guide is a commentary on biblical terms that appear to ascribe corporeal qualities to God; the result of literal interpretation is a material conception of God.
SEP: like Aquinas, Maimonides believes it is impossible to show by logical considerations whether the world was created or eternal; creation, though not demonstrated, is preferable.
SEP: no plurality of attributes in God; God is powerful should be taken as God is not lacking in power (GP 1.58); God's power bears no likeness to ours.
SEP: the more you can prove inapplicable to God, the better; citing Psalm 65, Maimonides concludes that the highest form of praise we can give God is silence.
SEP: the Guide has long been considered controversial and in some rabbinic circles was originally banned; question whether its reading owes more to Aristotle and Alfarabi than to Moses.
SEP Aquinas: the undergraduate arts faculty, whose curriculum consisted largely in the works of Aristotle.
SEP Aquinas (ca. 1225-1274): Dominican friar, taught in Paris; IEP: Dominican theologian at Paris drawing on Aristotle within Christian theology.
SEP: he wrote commentaries on all of Aristotle's principal works, with confidence that progress in philosophy will only benefit the Christian faith.
IEP Aquinas: truths apprehended by reason apart from revelation, e.g. that God exists and that there is one God (preambles to the faith), and truths such as the Trinity requiring grace.
IEP: although the faith takes us beyond what natural reason by itself can apprehend, according to Thomas it never contradicts what we know by way of natural reason.

SEP quotes Comm. Boethius De trinitate 2.3c: if anything is found in the words of the philosophers that is contrary to the faith, this is not philosophy but rather an abuse of philosophy, due to a failure of reason.
SEP: in On the Eternity of the World Aquinas concluded that no demonstrative argument is possible either way; that we think otherwise is a deliverance of the faith.

Summa I q13 a2: God lives means God is not like an inanimate thing, taught by Rabbi Moses; Aquinas: God is good means whatever good we attribute to creatures pre-exists in God, in a more excellent and higher way.

SEP: among the 219 articles condemned in Paris in 1277 a significant number seem to implicate Aquinas; promulgated three years to the day after his death; the Franciscan William de la Mare's Correctorium gave corrections, answered by his disciples.
SEP Wang Yangming (1472-1529): Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher; a leading critic of the orthodox Neo-Confucianism of Zhu Xi.
SEP quotes Wang: Qian investigated the bamboos in front of the pavilion and on the third day took sick; I myself tried and on the seventh day I also became sick.
SEP: exiled to a post in what is now Guizhou Province, he achieved a deep philosophical awakening (1508).
SEP quotes Wang: those who know but do not act simply do not yet know; one cannot say he knows filial piety simply because he knows how to say something filial.
SEP: Wang appropriates the Great Learning's image that hating evil is like hating a hateful odor; to recognize an odor as disgusting is to be repulsed by it.
SEP: Zhu Xi, along with Western philosophers like Aristotle, would accept the plagiarist's description (akrasia); objection: recognizing someone as attractive does not always result in action.
SEP Descartes' Epistemology quotes the basket of apples analogy: tip the whole lot out, then put back only those seen to be sound.
SEP quotes Meditations AT 7:18: for rejecting all my opinions it will be enough if I find in each of them at least some reason for doubt.
SEP quotes Med. 1: whether I am awake or asleep, two and three added together are five.
SEP quotes Med. 1: some malicious demon of the utmost power and cunning has employed all his energies in order to deceive me.
SEP quotes AT 7:25: I too undoubtedly exist, if he is deceiving me; this proposition, I am, I exist, is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind.

SEP Descartes: Discourse (in French, 1637), Principles (in Latin, 1644); SEP Epistemology: cogito ergo sum does not expressly appear in the Meditations; Wikipedia: je pense, donc je suis in the Discourse, later Latin in the Principles.

SEP quotes Gassendi (Fifth Objections): why consider everything false and imagine a deceiving God or evil demon, when citing the weakness of our nature would suffice; Descartes replies about preconceived opinions.

SEP Rationalism vs. Empiricism: most rationalists claim concepts and knowledge are gained independently of sense experience; Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz are the Continental Rationalists; such schemes should be adopted with great caution.
SEP Spinoza: born in 1632 in Amsterdam; the Ethics sets out definitions and axioms and then demonstrated propositions.

SEP: there is only one substance in the universe; it is God; everything else is in God; 'That eternal and infinite being we call God, or Nature, acts from the same necessity from which he exists' (IV, Preface).
SEP Leibniz (1646-1716): PSR, nothing happens without it being possible to give a reason why it is so and not otherwise.
SEP Leibniz on the Problem of Evil: the famous doctrine that this world is the best of all possible worlds, expressing God's goodness to the greatest extent possible.
SEP: Voltaire's Candide (1759) features Dr. Pangloss, whose refusal to acknowledge the badness of things caricatures Leibniz's optimism; evils may contribute to the world's excellence.
SEP Locke: the Essay (1689) Book I argues we have no innate knowledge; at birth the mind is a sort of blank slate; all ideas come from experience.
SEP Berkeley quotes PHK 1: a certain colour, taste, smell, figure and consistence observed to go together are signified by the name apple; he holds there are no mind-independent things.
SEP: esse est percipi (aut percipere), to be is to be perceived (or to perceive).

SEP: the objection that there are no trees in the Quad when no one perceives them; another strategy suggested by Berkeley's reference to some other spirit: God's perception guarantees continued existence.
Enquiry (Gutenberg): perceptions divided into less forcible and lively ideas and impressions; when we think of a golden mountain, we only join two consistent ideas, gold and mountain.
Enquiry: a person acquainted with all colours except one shade of blue could, few would deny, supply this deficiency; though this instance is so singular that it is scarcely worth observing.

SEP: where Locke puts forth the mind as a blank slate, Leibniz's New Essays offers a block of marble whose veins determine what figures it will accept; the mind plays a role in determining its contents.
SEP Kant and Hume on Causality quotes the Prolegomena: the remembrance of David Hume first interrupted my dogmatic slumber; SEP Kant: 1724-1804.
IEP Kant: Metaphysics: Hume maintains we cannot provide a priori or a posteriori justifications for beliefs like every event must have a cause.

SEP Kant quotes the Critique: up to now it has been assumed that all our cognition must conform to the objects; try assuming that objects must conform to our cognition, like the first thoughts of Copernicus.
SEP Kant: a priori knowledge is possible only because the sensible world depends on how the mind structures experience: sensibility gives space and time, understanding gives concepts such as cause.
IEP Kant: Metaphysics quotes B75: Thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind; against the passive empty theater or blank slate of both traditions.
SEP Transcendental Idealism: objects in space and time are appearances, and we know nothing of substance about things in themselves.
SEP Jacobi: his dictum that without that presupposition of the thing in itself he could not enter Kant's system, but with it could not stay within it.
IEP Avicenna: the flying man argument raises an objection which may also be levelled at Descartes: how do we know that the knowing subject is the self?
IEP Occasionalism: the claim that we see only succession is most commonly identified with Hume, but was first advanced by al-Baqillani in the 10th century and reiterated by al-Ghazali.
SEP Analysis of Knowledge: S knows that p iff p is true, S believes that p, and S is justified in believing that p; the JTB analysis, for justified true belief.
SEP: most epistemologists agree that what is false cannot be known; eighty-four is not a prime number; truth is a matter of how things are, not how they can be shown to be.
SEP: knowledge is a kind of relationship with the truth; the belief condition's idea is that you can only know what you believe.
SEP: William flips a coin and confidently believes on no particular basis that it will land tails; such a lucky guess can't count as knowledge, hence the justification condition.
SEP: the need for justification is often traced to Plato's Theaetetus, where a lawyer employing sophistry induces a jury into a true belief that is not knowledge.
IEP Knowledge: among epistemologically heterodox views, knowledge need not be anything beyond a true belief (Sartwell 1991; 1992); few epistemologists will accept so.
IEP Gettier Problems: Gettier discovered them in 1963; beliefs true and well supported by evidence yet, according to almost all epistemologists, not knowledge.
IEP: Smith and Jones applied for a job; the company president told Smith Jones will win; Smith counted ten coins in Jones's pocket and infers whoever gets the job has ten coins in their pocket.
IEP Case I: Smith himself gets the job and happens to have ten coins in his pocket, so his justified true belief is true by luck and fails to be knowledge.
IEP: Gettier's article had a dramatic impact, with almost all agreeing he had refuted the traditional definition; many attempts to repair it, including adding a fourth condition.
SEP: adding 'not inferred from any falsehood' is not widely accepted, since there are Gettier cases that need involve no inference; IEP cites Feldman 1974 on cases with no false evidence.
IEP: sheep in the field (Chisholm): you see what looks exactly like a sheep, really a dog disguised as a sheep; you are right because a sheep is behind the hill.
SEP Pyrrho: lived from around 365-360 BCE until around 275-270 BCE; Pyrrho wrote nothing, so his philosophy is reconstructed from reports by others.
SEP Sextus Empiricus: living probably in the second or third century CE; the Outlines of Pyrrhonism is the best and fullest account of Pyrrhonian skepticism, named for Pyrrho.
SEP: the Pyrrhonian skeptic has the skill of finding for every argument an equal and opposing argument, bringing suspension of judgment and ultimately tranquillity.
SEP: the phrases Skeptics use to indicate their suspension of judgment ('No more this than that', 'I determine nothing').
SEP quotes Sextus: Apelles, unable to represent the lather on a horse's mouth, flung his colour-wiping sponge at the picture, and it produced the effect.
SEP Ancient Skepticism: the most widely discussed charge is that they cannot act without belief (Apraxia Charge); skeptics describe their actions as guided by appearances.
SEP quotes PH I 24: by nature's guidance we perceive and think; by necessitation of feelings hunger conducts us to food; by handing down of customs and laws; by teaching of kinds of expertise.
IEP Brain in a Vat: a brain hooked to a computer that perfectly simulates experience; if I know that P (snow is white) then I know I am not a BIV; I do not know that; thus I do not know P.
IEP: the Brain in a Vat Argument is usually taken to be a modern version of Descartes's evil demon who systematically deceives us.
Putnam, Reason, Truth and History ch. 1: an ant by pure chance traces a caricature of Winston Churchill; most people would say it has not depicted him, having never seen Churchill.
IEP: (CC) a term refers to an object only if there is an appropriate causal connection between that term and the object.

Putnam: perhaps no evil scientist, only automatic machinery tending a vat of all sentient beings; the supposition cannot be true because it is self-refuting, like the thesis that all general statements are false.
IEP: Wright (1994) argues the argument does not affect certain versions of the Cartesian nightmare, such as my brain being taken out of my skull last night and hooked up to a computer.
IEP A Priori: knowable independent of any experience other than learning the language; a posteriori known on the basis of experience; all bachelors are unmarried vs it is raining outside now.
IEP lists water is H2O and dinosaurs existed as a posteriori, against cubes have six sides; if today is Tuesday then not Thursday; seven plus five equals twelve.
IEP: for such claims the reasons do not derive from experience; I seem able to see they are true by reflecting on their content; accounts of a priori justification relying on pure thought.
SEP Mill 3.4: amongst the Laws of Nature learnt by inductive reasoning are the laws of geometry and arithmetic.

Jeff Speaks (Notre Dame) handout: on Ayer's reading Mill made mathematical truths contingent empirical generalizations that could in principle be false; Ayer argues Mill mistakes their nature. Wikipedia Philosophy of mathematics: Ayer criticized Mill for making 2 + 2 = 4 uncertain and contingent.
Enquiry: That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction than the affirmation, that it will rise.
Enquiry: does it follow that other bread must also nourish me at another time...? The consequence seems nowise necessary.
SEP Problem of Induction: two types of argument, demonstrative and probable, neither will serve; Enquiry: going in a circle, and taking that for granted, which is the very point in question.
Enquiry: flame and heat always conjoined, the mind is carried by custom to expect heat; Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.

SEP: Reichenbach thought Hume's argument unassailable but offered a weaker pragmatic vindication, comparing a physician: I do not know whether an operation will save the man, but if there is any remedy, it is an operation.
IEP Nyaya: perception is commonly called the eldest knowledge source, since other pramanas depend on perceptual input.
IEP: testimony is the assertion of a qualified speaker; Vatsyayana: an apta possesses direct knowledge and willingness to convey it without distortion.
IEP: analogy is framed as a means of vocabulary acquisition; the standard example: told a water buffalo looks like a cow, later recognizes one in the countryside.
IEP: fire on the hill (thesis); smoke on the hill (reason); wherever smoke, fire, like a kitchen hearth and unlike a lake; this hill is likewise smoky; therefore fire.
IEP: in the language of Nyaya, fire pervades smoke; an epistemic pervasion: we never find smoke instances without fire instances.
SEP Epistemology in Classical Indian Philosophy: inference depends upon generalizations which outstrip perceptual evidence, everything F as a G; no one can know that, Carvaka claims.
SEP: the standard response is pragmatic: we could not act as we do without inference; the skeptic relies on generalizations when he voices skepticism, using words with repeatable meanings (Gangesa).
